# Understanding MoleculeNet

In this post we will describe MoleculeNet and explore one of its datasets.

## What is MoleculeNet?

For any molecule, we can ask questions about its properties: How soluble is it in water? Can it cross the blood-brain barrier? Does it inhibit a particular protein? Does it produce a response in a toxicity-related assay?

These are examples of **molecular property prediction**. MoleculeNet is a collection of benchmark datasets and evaluation conventions designed to help researchers compare molecular machine learning approaches. It is not one dataset or one uniform CSV file.

Zhenqin Wu and colleagues introduced it in the 2018 paper [*MoleculeNet: a benchmark for molecular machine learning*](https://doi.org/10.1039/C7SC02664A), published in *Chemical Science*, 9, 513-530 [1]. The original collection contains **17 datasets across four scientific categories**.


![Moleculenet categories](data:image/png;base64,)






## Five sources to keep in mind


### 📄 [Original MoleculeNet paper](https://doi.org/10.1039/C7SC02664A)

The benchmark specification. Use it for the original 17 datasets, scientific motivation, recommended splits, and metrics. [1]


### 📘 [DeepChem API documentation](https://deepchem.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api_reference/moleculenet.html)

The practical loader reference: functions, target columns, preprocessing, and parameters. It also includes datasets beyond the original seventeen. [2]


### 💻 [DeepChem MoleculeNet repository](https://github.com/deepchem/moleculenet)

A benchmark tutorial, examples, and historical comparison material. It is not a complete store of the raw scientific data. [3]


### 🤗 [Hugging Face benchmark](https://huggingface.co/datasets/katielink/moleculenet-benchmark)

A packaged subset with ten configurations: BACE, BBBP, ClinTox, ESOL, FreeSolv, HIV, Lipophilicity, QM9, SIDER, and Tox21. The card maps train, test, and val to CSV files; validation files are named valid.csv. Inspect split provenance before comparing scores. [4]


### 🎓 [DeepChem introduction tutorial](https://deepchem.io/tutorials/an-introduction-to-moleculenet/)

A guided starting point for loading and navigating data.[5]







## What is SMILES?

Most MoleculeNet's dataset have input in form of **SMILES**. **SMILES** stands for *Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System*. A SMILES string is a text representation of a molecular structure. Consider ethanol:


![Ethanol](data:image/png;base64,)


A molecule is not the same as its SMILES string. For example, `CCO` and `OCC` describe the same ethanol connectivity. Ordinary SMILES specifies connectivity and can encode some stereochemistry, but it does not specify an exact three-dimensional conformation.

For machine learning, the structure can be converted into a Morgan fingerprint, a molecular graph, or a token sequence for a molecular language model such as ChemBERTa.

## What is a task?

Every dataset in MoleculeNet is about solving one or multiplel tasks. A **task** is a specific property or biological endpoint to predict.
| Example | Samples | Tasks | Targets per sample |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|
| Solubility measured for 1,000 molecules | 1,000 | 1 | One number |
| Activity assessed in 12 assays for 1,000 molecules | 1,000 | 12 | Up to 12 binary labels |

The second example is **multitask prediction**. Twelve binary tasks are not the same as one problem with twelve mutually exclusive classes. A molecule may be active in several assays, inactive in others, and unmeasured in the rest.

## Catalogue of the original 17 datasets

The following tables reproduce the counts, task numbers, prediction types, recommended splits, and metrics reported in **Table 1 of the original paper** [1]. They are historical benchmark specifications, not verified row counts for a current download. Later releases and loader settings can differ.

### Quantum mechanics: 4 datasets

These datasets contain properties calculated using quantum chemistry. The original paper lists three-dimensional coordinates for all four, and lists QM7b with 3D coordinates rather than SMILES.

| Dataset | Records | Tasks | Type | Split | Metric |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|:--|:--|
| QM7 | 7,165 | 1 | Regression | Stratified | MAE |
| QM7b | 7,211 | 14 | Regression | Random | MAE |
| QM8 | 21,786 | 12 | Regression | Random | MAE |
| QM9 | 133,885 | 12 | Regression | Random | MAE |

### Physical chemistry: 3 datasets

These describe solubility, hydration, and partitioning between liquid phases. All three are suitable starting points for molecular regression.

| Dataset | Records | Tasks | Type | Split | Metric |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|:--|:--|
| ESOL | 1,128 | 1 | Regression | Random | RMSE |
| FreeSolv | 643 | 1 | Regression | Random | RMSE |
| Lipophilicity | 4,200 | 1 | Regression | Random | RMSE |

### Biophysics: 5 datasets

These concern biological activity and protein interactions. PDBbind records are protein-ligand complexes; its count should not be interpreted as a count of unique isolated molecules.

| Dataset | Records | Tasks | Type | Split | Metric |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|:--|:--|
| PCBA | 439,863 | 128 | Classification | Random | PR-AUC |
| MUV | 93,127 | 17 | Classification | Random | PR-AUC |
| HIV | 41,913 | 1 | Classification | Scaffold | ROC-AUC |
| PDBbind | 11,908 | 1 | Regression | Time | RMSE |
| BACE | 1,522 | 1 | Classification | Scaffold | ROC-AUC |

### Physiology: 5 datasets

These concern biological effects, drug behavior, and toxicity-related outcomes.

| Dataset | Records | Tasks | Type | Split | Metric |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|:--|:--|
| BBBP | 2,053 | 1 | Classification | Scaffold | ROC-AUC |
| Tox21 | 8,014 | 12 | Classification | Random | ROC-AUC |
| ToxCast | 8,615 | 617 | Classification | Random | ROC-AUC |
| SIDER | 1,427 | 27 | Classification | Random | ROC-AUC |
| ClinTox | 1,491 | 2 | Classification | Random | ROC-AUC |



## What does each dataset predict?

### Quantum mechanics: electronic and energetic properties

Quantum chemistry concerns electrons, energy, and molecular structure. Instead of asking whether a molecule dissolves in water, we might ask how its electrons respond to an electric field.

Geometry is part of these datasets' scientific context. A SMILES-only model can still be evaluated, but its input is different from that of a model receiving 3D coordinates. QM9 is a useful later study; QM7b is not a straightforward SMILES-based starting point.


| Dataset | Interpretation of the targets |
|:--|:--|
| **QM7** | Atomization energy: an energy difference between a molecule and its separated atoms. Check the dataset's sign convention before interpreting values. |
| **QM7b** | Fourteen calculated properties, including energetic and electronic quantities obtained at different levels of theory. |
| **QM8** | Excitation energies **and oscillator strengths** for electronic transitions, evaluated with multiple quantum-chemical methods. Oscillator strengths describe transition intensity, not energy. |
| **QM9** | Twelve benchmark properties covering electronic, energetic, and thermodynamic behavior, including dipole moment, polarizability, orbital energies, and heat capacity. |




### Physical chemistry: practical molecular properties

#### ESOL: water solubility

**Question:** How much of a chemical dissolves in water at equilibrium?


![Esol](data:image/png;base64,)


The target is measured base-10 logarithmic molar solubility. Lower values mean lower solubility. ESOL is also called the **Delaney dataset**.

#### FreeSolv: hydration free energy

**Question:** What free-energy change accompanies transfer of a molecule from the gas phase into water?


![Freesolv](data:image/png;base64,)


The experimental hydration free energy is the regression target, commonly reported in kcal/mol. A more negative value represents more favorable hydration under the stated conventions.

#### Lipophilicity: distribution between octanol and water

**Question:** How does a compound distribute between an organic phase and water?


![Lipophilicity](data:image/png;base64,)


The target is experimental **logD at pH 7.4**. A higher value indicates greater distribution into octanol relative to water. Unlike logP for the neutral form, logD includes ionized and neutral species at the specified pH. The target definitions and loader options are described in DeepChem's reference [2].

### Biophysics: biological activity and binding

An **assay** is an experimental procedure that measures a particular biological response. Its activity label is specific to that procedure and its labeling rules.

| Dataset | Interpretation of the labels |
|:--|:--|
| **PCBA** | Active or inactive outcomes across 128 PubChem screening assays; not every molecule has every outcome. |
| **MUV** | Activity labels for 17 curated virtual-screening tasks with very rare positives. |
| **HIV** | Whether a compound shows activity in an assay of HIV replication inhibition. |
| **PDBbind** | A numerical experimental binding-affinity target for a protein-ligand complex, commonly represented on a negative-log scale. Check the release and affinity definition. |
| **BACE** | A binary activity label for inhibition of human BACE-1, an enzyme. |

PCBA and MUV emphasize precision-recall evaluation because identifying rare active compounds is central to screening. HIV's original categories distinguish confirmed active, moderately active, and inactive compounds; MoleculeNet merges the two active groups into one positive class.

BACE also supports regression in DeepChem [2]. That is a distinct target choice from the original classification benchmark. 

#### Why PDBbind is different


![Pdbbind](data:image/png;base64,)


Binding affinity is not a property of the ligand alone: a molecule can bind differently to different proteins. A ligand-only Morgan fingerprint does not encode the complete complex. We should keep PDBbind separate from the first SMILES-only comparison.

### Physiology and toxicology: biological consequences

| Dataset | Interpretation of the labels |
|:--|:--|
| **BBBP** | Whether the compound is labeled as penetrating the blood-brain barrier. |
| **Tox21** | Activity in twelve toxicity-related assays involving nuclear receptors and stress-response pathways. |
| **ToxCast** | Outcomes for 617 high-throughput toxicology assay tasks. |
| **SIDER** | Recorded adverse-effect associations grouped into 27 system-organ categories. |
| **ClinTox** | Two binary targets: FDA approval status and clinical-trial toxicity. |

**Tox21 is not a direct human-safety test.** Activity in a pathway-related assay is not proof of harm in humans.

**SIDER describes recorded associations.** Its labels do not give the probability that a particular patient will experience an adverse effect.

**ClinTox has two distinct endpoints.** Approval status is not interchangeable with a toxicity outcome. The two labels must remain separate prediction tasks.

## How the data are organized in practice

Three levels connect source files to a model:

| Level | What it contains | What to inspect |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **1. Source data** | CSV, SDF, MAT, or other files containing structures, identifiers, and targets | Which column or field describes the structure? Which measurements are the targets? |
| **2. Benchmark preparation** | Selected targets, filtering, standardization, and train/validation/test membership | Which records changed or disappeared? How were partitions created? |
| **3. Model input** | Fingerprints, graphs, embeddings, or tokenized SMILES | Which representation and parameters were used? |

DeepChem wraps data in dataset objects: `X` stores inputs, `y` stores targets, `w` stores weights and can mask missing labels, and `ids` stores identifiers, often SMILES. For N samples and T tasks, `y` and `w` commonly have shape `(N, T)`. The shape of `X` depends on the representation. Loader-returned transformers may normalize targets or reweight classes [2].

Keep record identity, labels, and split membership aligned when changing representations. This is essential for a fair Morgan-versus-ChemBERTa comparison.

## Why dataset sizes differ across sources

The original paper, a downloaded CSV, and a featurized dataset can report different counts. For example:

| Dataset | Original paper | Later reported count | How to interpret the comparison |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|
| BACE | 1,522 | 1,513 | DeepChem's classification loader documents the latter count [2]. |
| Tox21 | 8,014 | 7,831 | A frequently used processed count; verify the particular release before treating it as your dataset size. |

These are not before-and-after counts from an audit performed here. Revisions, filtering, invalid structures, and duplicate handling can change counts, but the cause of a particular difference must be traced to that release's processing history.

For experiments, record the download source and revision, source row count, usable record count, exclusions, and final partition sizes. Do not silently substitute a newer count into a table describing the original paper.



## How should the data be split?

The **training set** fits model parameters. The **validation set** helps choose settings and models. The **test set** estimates performance after those choices are fixed.

| Strategy | How it works | What it probes |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Random** | Assigns records randomly to partitions | Performance when training and test chemistry may be similar |
| **Scaffold** | Groups molecules by a defined molecular core and assigns groups to partitions | Generalization to different core structures |
| **Time** | Trains on earlier records and evaluates on later ones | Generalization to subsequently collected data |
| **Stratified** | Balances a chosen label distribution across partitions | Performance while controlling target-distribution imbalance |

The original QM7 stratification concerns a continuous regression target; it should not be confused with ordinary class-balanced splitting.

Scaffold splitting often creates a harder structural-generalization problem, but difficulty depends on the data and implementation. Different scaffolds do not guarantee that all molecules across partitions are chemically dissimilar. Duplicate handling also needs a defined policy before splitting.

For model comparisons, freeze the exact record IDs in each partition. Use training data to fit preprocessing transformations; keep the test set out of model selection.

## Which datasets should we prioritize?

For a comparison between Morgan fingerprints and pretrained molecular models such as ChemBERTa, the following progression keeps the early experiments manageable:

| Priority | Datasets | Reason |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **1** | ESOL | Learn single-target regression and target units |
| **2** | BBBP | Learn binary labels, imbalance, and probability-based evaluation |
| **3** | FreeSolv, Lipophilicity | Compare regression across distinct physical properties |
| **4** | BACE, HIV | Explore biological activity classification |
| **5** | Tox21 | Introduce multitask prediction and missing-label masks |
| **6** | ClinTox, SIDER | Study distinct outcome definitions and challenging labels |
| **Later** | PCBA, MUV, ToxCast | Scale to sparse or highly imbalanced multitask screening |
| **Separate study** | QM7, QM7b, QM8, QM9, PDBbind | Account explicitly for geometry or protein context |
